items.title: Sofia Coppola's Near-Perfect Cult Classic Follow-Up Is Officially Streaming
items.summary: You know that you really are a film buff when you realize that the release you have been looking forward to the most is a documentary — and not the one everybody is talking about. In October, MUBI released Making Marie Antoinette , a movie about the making of Sofia Coppola 's Marie Antoinette , directed by her own mother, Eleanor Coppola , during lockdown. The matriarch of the famous filmmaking clan is best known for directing Hearts of Darkness: A Filmmaker's Apocalypse , another making-of documentary depicting the chaotic production of her husband Francis Ford Coppola 's classic Apocalypse Now . Surprisingly enough, however, both movies have much more in common beyond simply being Coppola family affairs, which makes Making Marie Antoinette just as compelling as its subject.
items.t: Sofia Coppola's Near-Perfect Cult Classic Follow-Up Is Officially Streaming

items.title: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step
items.summary:
The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering

Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower?

But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride, has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. Yet they still keep coming (IP is king) and before the inevitable Shrek legacy sequel hits cinemas next summer, Netflix is trying to conjure up that same mix of snark and sentiment with Steps, a Cinderella story but, wait for it, not the Cinderella story you thought you knew…
items.t: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step

items.title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
items.summary:
The Russian film-maker spent 40 days in a coma and suffered 92% lung damage during the pandemic. He describes how making new movie Minotaur helped his rehabilitation

Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.”

Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma. He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile

items.title: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return
items.summary:
David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script, picking up from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, and its lead is more ineffably beguiling than ever

We got through to the very end of Quentin Tarantino’s previous film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood without finding out exactly how, why or if Brad Pitt’s stuntman character Cliff Booth murdered his wife. It was an issue only addressed in Tarantino’s novel based on the movie. And throughout the 140 minutes of this outrageous sugar-rush sequel – scripted by Tarantino and directed by David Fincher – this subject is tactfully passed over in silence, the one point that damages our perception of Cliff’s amiable-cowpoke good nature.

Cliff is the guy who climaxed the previous picture by helping with a dramatic rescue; after, that is, gallantly refusing an age-gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. Well, we may not get the complete picture of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover Cliff Booth novel, with which this film is to form a kind of multimedia narrative event. But there is nonetheless such a huge amount of energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste and film-making style to be had here.

Continue reading...
items.t: The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth review – Tarantino and Fincher join forces for Brad Pitt’s glorious return

items.title: Alex Cox: ‘John Lydon said Sid and Nancy was a nightmarish piece of garbage’
items.summary:
The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson

Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam’s version? AwapBamBoogers
No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards.

The giant boar in Razorback gave me nightmares when I saw it on Moviedrome. Did it give you nightmares too? Sootsayer
I don’t remember. The films in Moviedrome were picked by [producer and director] Nick Freand Jones, who had access to all the films the BBC had under…

items.title: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw
items.summary:
Pattinson is a character actor whose talent for inscrutable appraisal may mean a new era for 007. Will this more willowy, classy Bond leave sexism in the shadows?

• New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson
• Share your thoughts on the casting
• Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond

If it wasn’t Bond … maybe it would have been Dr No in some hi-tech reboot. But Robert Pattinson – with his movie-star chops and track record in hip A24-type character turns, and his gift for cool, inscrutable appraisal and sensual menace – is an exquisite choice as 007, playing on the darker and more sophisticated notes of Pattinson’s performing personality.

And let’s hope, incidentally, that the actor now isn’t forced into a five-hour daily gym regimen to bulk up. I like the taller and more willowy Bond that Pattinson represents, the Bond from whose frame the tux hangs gracefully, the Bond with elegant abandon who’s a former British Naval officer, not a former US Navy Seal, the Bond who with a crinkly-eyed reptilian grin can style out waking up with a hangover after too many whisky-and-sodas at the baccarat table.
items.t: Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond | Peter Bradshaw

items.title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
items.summary:
The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track?

What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022, when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings. But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, the plan was James Gunn.

Fast forward four years, and that plan lies in tatters. Gunn and his fellow DC Studios CEO Peter Safran have this week been fired (though they will reportedly stay on as film-makers), and Jeremy Latcham, another former Marvel man, is the new boss. What is the plan now? Nobody seems to know, and there is not much point asking David Ellison, the man whose Skydance empire has now gobbled up two of the former big five Hollywood studios (Paramount last year and Warner…
items.t: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years
